=== 58000 - Eolian Comments on Proposed Transmission Cost Allocation Rules.pdf ===
                                           PROJECT NO. 58000

    RULEMAKING TO UPDATE                                §       PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION
    WHOLESALE AND IOU RETAIL                            §                OF TEXAS
    TRANSMISSION COST RECOVERY                          §
    IN THE ERCOT REGION

                                     COMMENTS OF EOLIAN, L.P.

         COMES NOW Eolian, L.P. (“Eolian”) and files these comments on proposed amendments

to 16 Texas Administrative Code (“TAC”) §§ 25.192 and 25.193 and proposed new § 25.252. The

proposal would implement Section 6 of Senate Bill (“SB”) 6 as enacted by the 89th Texas

Legislature by revising wholesale and retail transmission cost recovery in the ERCOT Region.

         Eolian is a Corporate Member of the Electric Reliability Council of Texas, Inc. (“ERCOT”)

and owns several certificated Power Generation Companies (“PGCs”) and ERCOT-registered

Resource Entities that operate Energy Storage Resources (“ESRs”) in the ERCOT Region. Eolian

is also developing a domestic critical primary metal production facility with expected peak demand

sufficient to qualify it as a "large load customer” under proposed § 25.194, relating to Large Load

Interconnection Standards. The facility would also qualify as a “critical load industrial customer”

under PURA § 17.002(3-b). 1 Accordingly, the proposed rules will directly affect the project’s

interconnection economics, transmission rate exposure, development, and long-term operating

costs.

         These changes are particularly consequential for traditional industrial and manufacturing

projects that compete in commodity markets. Large computational loads (“LCLs”), including

hyperscale data centers, may have project economics capable of supporting materially higher

overall electricity delivery costs than facilities producing critical metal metals. New domestic


1
     Public Utility Regulatory Act, Tex. Util. Code Ann. §§ 11.001-66.016 (PURA) § 17.002(3-b) defines Critical
     Load Industrial Customer as “an industrial customer for whom an interruption or suspension of electric service
     will create a dangerous or life-threatening condition on the customer's premises.”
 aluminum, steel, copper, magnesium, and similar facilities must compete not only with projects in

other U.S. power markets, but also with overseas production that may benefit from lower-cost or

subsidized legacy electricity supply. A transmission rate design that imposes the same new, long-

term fixed costs on all large loads can therefore have materially different investment effects across

customer types.

        As the Commission addresses the consumer-cost and stranded-infrastructure risks

associated with rapid growth in data center demand, it should avoid reforms that unintentionally

deter investment in the traditional industrial economy that Texas is also seeking to expand. The

nationwide buildout of artificial intelligence (“AI”) infrastructure will itself depend on substantial

domestic production of critical metals and other physical inputs. The Commission should therefore

distinguish LCLs from critical industrial loads when objective differences in operating

characteristics, cost causation, or transmission system impacts warrant different treatment, rather

than allowing policies developed principally in response to computational-load growth to impose

the same incremental burdens on traditional industrial projects that do not create the same risks.

       The proposed large load provisions would impose several significant and interrelated

obligations on a new interconnecting industrial project. Proposed § 25.193(d) would establish a

minimum transmission billing demand equal to the greatest of contracted peak demand, the

customer's highest non-coincident peak (“NCP”) demand in the preceding year, or the customer's

12 coincident peak (“12CP”) demand. Proposed §§ 25.193(d)(3) and 25.252(e) would begin billing

when transmission capacity is made available, even if the customer has not energized or is not

fully using that capacity, and would maintain the minimum billing demand for at least 20 years.

At the same time, proposed § 25.252 would require direct cash contributions in aid of construction

(“CIAC”) for transmission and distribution interconnection costs, prohibit interconnection




                                                                           Eolian Comments – Page 2
 allowances, require a long-term interconnection agreement, and incorporate the financial

commitments required by §25.194.

       For a capital-intensive industrial project that must make siting, procurement, financing, and

construction decisions years before reaching full production, these requirements create material

fixed-cost and timing risks. A project may become responsible for substantial transmission charges

before it is capable of using the available capacity, while also funding directly assigned

interconnection facilities and maintaining financial security intended to protect against stranded

infrastructure. The Commission should therefore evaluate the minimum billing demand together

with the other financial protections imposed on new large loads and should avoid layering

overlapping mechanisms that recover the same underlying stranded-cost risk more than once.

       Proposed § 25.193(e) creates an additional allocation risk by authorizing an investor-

owned utility (“IOU”) distribution service provider (“DSP”) to request adjustments that increase

billing units associated with anticipated large load customers and increase the allocation of costs

to classes that include those customers. Any such anticipatory adjustment should be subject to

transparent data standards, notice, and a prompt true-up to actual service and billing responsibility.

A new industrial customer or its rate class should not bear forecast-based transmission costs for

capacity that has not yet become available or for load that does not materialize.

       The governing principle should be cost causation, not an assumed ability to pay. SB 6

directs the Commission to determine whether transmission charges appropriately assign the costs

of transmission investment; it does not prescribe Staff's proposed 20-year, greatest-of minimum

billing demand. PURA §§ 36.001 and 36.003 authorize reasonable customer classifications and

rate design, but require rates to remain just, reasonable, equitable, and not unreasonably

preferential, prejudicial, or discriminatory. PURA § 37.0561(b) likewise directs the Commission




                                                                           Eolian Comments – Page 3
 to establish large load interconnection standards in a manner designed to support business

development in Texas while minimizing stranded infrastructure costs and maintaining reliability.

Those requirements support targeted treatment based on demonstrable cost and service

characteristics; they do not support imposing the same long-term fixed billing construct on

materially different types of large loads merely because each exceeds the statutory large load

threshold.

        This distinction is particularly important for traditional industrial and manufacturing

facilities. The record in Project No. 58484 identified circumstances in which large computational

loads may present rapid ramping, trip, power-electronic, or other stability characteristics that can

drive specialized transmission investment. 2 Traditional industrial loads may present materially

different operating characteristics and development risks. Any special rate treatment should

recognize those differences and should also recognize verifiable mitigation, including on-site

generation, storage, ramp controls, or other measures that reduce the customer's net impact on the

transmission system. The Commission should not base transmission rate treatment on assumptions

regarding profitability or willingness to pay. Any Commission policy or rule changes must

recognize that some industries that are willing to pay extraordinarily high all-in prices for

electricity must not inhibit industrial growth across the remainder of the Texas economy.

        Eolian limits these comments to Commission Staff’s Questions 1, 2 and 4 and the

implementation issues directly related to those questions.




2
    See Project No. 58484, Comments of Eolian, L.P. at 2 and 6 (Sept. 9, 2025) (describing rapid and frequent
    ramping, sudden trips, and specialized stability-driven upgrades associated with large data center loads); Proposal
    for Publication, supra note 1, at 6–7 (Question No. 4).


                                                                                        Eolian Comments – Page 4
                            RESPONSES TO SPECIFIC QUESTIONS

1.     Should the values associated with the large load minimum billing demand provisions
       be different for large load customers with different contracted peak demands or
       different non-coincident (NCP) demands?

       Yes, if the Commission retains a large load minimum billing demand, the applicable values

should be calibrated to the cost and stranded-infrastructure risk presented by the customer rather

than imposed as a uniform 100% floor based solely on contracted peak demand or NCP demand.

Different load sizes and operating profiles can create materially different risks, but load size alone

is not a sufficient proxy for cost causation. The Commission should use objective criteria that

account for the customer's reserved capacity, expected ramp, directly assigned interconnection

costs, financial security, and demonstrated operating characteristics.

       The implementation of minimum charges based solely on peak demand or exposure to NCP

demand would create a disincentive to adjust load exposure during the most critical hours of the

day. For example, if a large baseload industrial facility can adjust its load during a critical morning

during a winter storm but is charged a flat annual minimum billing demand amount based on peak

annual demand, the facility will have less incentive to adjust its processes for those critical peak

hours even though their demand reduction actions would provide a disproportionate value to grid

reliability and would help keep energy costs lower during the whether event.

       The proposed formula in § 25.193(d)(2) would set the minimum billing demand at the

greatest of contracted peak demand, the highest NCP demand in the preceding year, or 12CP

demand. For a new project, contracted peak demand may therefore become the effective floor

before the project has established any operating history. Combined with proposed §§ 25.193(d)(3)

and 25.252(e), which commence billing when capacity is available rather than when the customer

has energized or reached its expected load, the proposal could require a new industrial customer




                                                                            Eolian Comments – Page 5
 to pay transmission charges based on its full reserved capacity during construction,

commissioning, or ramp-up. 3 That exposure is not necessarily proportional to the transmission

costs the customer is causing during those periods.

        A contracted demand floor can also weaken efficient demand response incentives. If an

industrial facility can reduce grid imports during critical periods but remains billed at its contracted

peak demand, the customer receives little or no transmission cost benefit from reducing demand

when the system is stressed. The same concern applies to investments in onsite generation, storage,

load controls, or other measures that lower the customer's net transmission usage. Eolian's

comments in Project No. 58484 emphasized that transmission rate design should preserve

incentives for efficient system use and should recognize mitigation measures that reduce system

impacts. 4 The Commission should preserve those incentives here rather than convert the minimum

billing demand into an unavoidable charge unrelated to actual or mitigated system use.

        The Commission should also avoid an ongoing rate distinction based solely on whether an

industrial customer happens to be a new entrant. Direct interconnection costs for a new large load

may appropriately be assigned to that customer under PURA § 35.004(c-1) and the Commission's

interconnection rules. 5 But once similarly situated customers are taking network service, newness

alone is not a cost-causation principle for permanently allocating network transmission costs.

Applying the new minimum billing demand to a new non-LCL industrial facility while similarly

situated incumbent industrial facilities remain outside that obligation would create a material

competitive disadvantage unrelated to differences in ongoing use of the transmission system.


3
    See PUC Proj. No. 58000, supra note 1, at 28–34 (proposed 16 TAC §§ 25.193(d)(2)–(3), 25.252(e)(1)–(2)).
4
    See PUC Proj. No. 58484, Eolian, L.P.’s Response to Commission Staff’s Recommendations, supra note 5, at 7–
    9; Comments of Eolian, L.P., supra note 4, at 3–6 (emphasizing predictable demand-response signals and
    recognition of measures that reduce net system impacts).
5
    See Tex. Util. Code § 35.004(c-1); Eolian, L.P.’s Response to Commission Staff’s Recommendations, supra note
    5, at 4–6; Texas Industrial Energy Consumers’ Comments at 4–6, Project No. 58484, Item No. 58 (Nov. 25,
    2025).


                                                                                   Eolian Comments – Page 6
          Accordingly, if the Commission retains a minimum billing demand, it should establish a

calibrated or ratcheted floor that reflects residual stranded-cost exposure after considering CIAC,

financial security, actual ramp, and other objectively verifiable mitigation. The rule should permit

the floor to decline as those risks decline and should apply comparable standards to similarly

situated customers. A uniform greatest-of contracted peak demand, NCP, or 12CP standard is too

blunt to accomplish those objectives.

2.       Should the large load minimum billing demand be:
         a.    fixed for 20 years as proposed;
         b.    reduced in phases over a period of 20 years; or
         c.    extended to a longer time period?

         Eolian does not support a fixed minimum billing demand for "no less than 20 years." For

a non-LCL industrial facility, the Commission should first determine whether a special minimum

billing demand is warranted at all. If the Commission nevertheless applies such a requirement,

Eolian could support option (b) – a defined phase-down over a period that does not exceed 20

years.

         As discussed below in response to Question No. 4, and as mentioned above, Eolian

respectfully submits that a new or interconnecting non-LCL industrial load should not be subject

to a materially different ongoing transmission cost allocation solely because it is an interconnecting

large load. Applying a new minimum billing demand only to new large loads while similarly

situated incumbent industrial loads remain outside that obligation would substantially increase

costs for new industrial and manufacturing projects to the benefit of incumbents and create an

immediate competitive disadvantage unrelated to differences in ongoing use of the transmission

system. If the Commission nevertheless applies a minimum billing demand to non-computational




                                                                           Eolian Comments – Page 7
 industrial loads, that obligation should decline as the stranded-infrastructure risk associated with

the new interconnection declines. 6

        The phased reduction should be administered on a known schedule based on established

and transparent criteria with a baseline calculation considering ALL large loads on the system that

that use and benefit from the transmission system. This would help ensure that incumbent large

loads that benefit from system upgrades and enhancements are not insulated from contributing to

system costs solely because they interconnected earlier. A phase-down is also more consistent with

the declining residual risk associated with an established operating facility and, over time, with the

depreciation of the project and transmission assets. In summary, the minimum billing demand

should operate as a time-limited cost-recovery mechanism for incremental, front-loaded,

customer-caused costs and risks that objectively diminish over time, rather than as a permanent

surcharge on new industrial development.

        In addition, reducing the minimum billing demand over time, with a corresponding greater

role for variable transmission charges, would preserve the incentive for large load customers to

develop onsite generation, storage, load controls, or other measures that reduce grid imports when

the transmission system is stressed. A fixed contracted demand floor can materially diminish the

transmission-cost benefit of those investments even when they reduce the customer’s actual system

impact. Any phase-down should therefore recognize objectively verifiable mitigation and actual

operating performance. 7

        The Commission should also recognize that the transmission system is a public good that

is used by all consumers, and as a practical matter, specific cost allocation to consumers is


6
    See PURA § 37.0561(h)–(j) (requiring financial-commitment standards and providing for release of security as
    load-ramp milestones are achieved, upon withdrawal, or when committed capacity is reallocated).
7
    See PURA § 37.0561(i); PUC Proj. No. 58484, Comments of Eolian, L.P., supra note 4, at 6; Eolian, L.P.’s
    Response to Commission Staff’s Recommendations, supra note 5, at 7–9.


                                                                                   Eolian Comments – Page 8
 functionally impossible. Importantly, any new transmission design system elements that must be

paid for by a new large load will actually be used by that customer as well as by incumbent large

loads and future customers. The biggest challenge of any proposed allocation of cost of new

transmission system elements to new large loads is that there will inevitably be a “free-ride”

problem. This essentially penalizes first movers and, in competitive market segments, can actually

discourage investment and innovation that benefit Texans overall. As a result, the Commission

should ensure that all large loads – new, incumbent, and future loads – contribute to the cost of

new transmission system infrastructure to help prevent the free-ride effect.

         Finally, the rule should provide a definite duration and a clear transition framework.

Proposed § 25.193(d)(3) states that the minimum billing demand applies for “no less than 20

years,” while proposed § 25.252(e)(2)(ii) refers to 240 consecutive payments during the first 20

years after billing commences. The final rule should establish a maximum period and specify how

the obligation applies to phased energization, changes in contracted demand, interruptions,

transfers, early retirement, and capacity that is reallocated or no longer available to serve the

project. It should also address projects that made substantial development or interconnection

commitments under existing tariffs before the new requirements become effective. Regulatory

timing, rather than cost causation, should not determine whether otherwise similarly situated

industrial projects face dramatically different long-term transmission obligations. 8

4.       Should separate rate treatment be applied to a large computational load, defined as
         an entity that is subject to § 25.194 of this title (relating to Large Load Interconnection
         Standards) and in which 50% or greater of the demand at the site consists of power
         electronic based load, specifically computational load, such as data centers and
         cryptocurrency mining facilities?


8
     See Proposal for Publication, supra note 1, at 28–34 (proposed 16 TAC §§ 25.193(d)(3), 25.252(e)(2)(ii)); see
     also id. at 16–17, 33–34 (proposed 16 TAC §§ 25.192(e)(6), 25.252(d), (f)); Act of June 20, 2025, 89th Leg.,
     R.S., ch. 953, § 7 (S.B. 6) (applying Tex. Util. Code § 35.004(c-1) to interconnection agreements entered into on
     or after S.B. 6’s effective date).


                                                                                       Eolian Comments – Page 9
          As noted previously, Eolian is currently in the process of developing a domestic critical

industrial metal production facility that will have an expected peak demand that would qualify it

as a "large load customer” within the meaning of PURA § 37.0561(c). 9 This facility will not be an

LCL which has been the primary focus of the implementation of SB 6. Transmission reforms

intended to address the challenges associated with unprecedented data center and computational

load growth should not inadvertently discourage investment in traditional industrial and

manufacturing facilities that strengthen domestic production.

         SB 6 required the Commission to begin evaluating the existing wholesale transmission cost

allocation methodology within 90 days after the bill took effect and, following completion of that

evaluation, must amend its rules by December 31, 2026, to ensure that wholesale transmission

charges appropriately allocate the costs of transmission investment.. 10 Staff’s proposal in this

proceeding is a direct result of that analysis in Project No. 58484, Evaluation of Transmission Cost

Recovery, and Staff’s Draft Report issued therein. 11 Although SB 6 facially applies to all large

loads in ERCOT, it is important to recall that the new large loads that triggered the Legislature to

adopt SB 6 and the need for the Commission’s study and these proposed rules was the development

of large data centers. Eolian’s facility is not a large data center but has been directly impacted by

the focus on those projects. As Eolian has pointed out before, the processes that the Commission

and ERCOT have been adopting for LCLs are not appropriate for the development of large

industrial facilities that are competing in a global commodity market. 12 This is yet another one of


9
     PURA § 37.0561 providing that, “The standards must apply only to customers requesting a new or expanded
     interconnection where the total load at a single site would exceed a demand threshold established by the
     commission based on the size of loads that significantly impact transmission needs in the ERCOT power region.”
10
     Senate Bill 6, § 6(a).
11
     PUC       Proj.    No.    58484,    Commission         Staff’s    Draft    Report     (May    4,  2026)     at
     https://interchange.puc.texas.gov/Documents/58484_117_1638123.PDF.
12
     PUC Proj. No. 58481, Rulemaking to Implement Large Load Interconnection Standards Under PURA § 37.0561,
     Comments of Eolian, L.P. on Proposed New TAC § 25.194, at 2-3 (Apr. 17, 2026) at
     https://interchange.puc.texas.gov/Documents/58481_187_1624295.PDF.


                                                                                    Eolian Comments – Page 10
 those situations. The impact of the proposed changes will mean that an industrial load trying to

locate in the ERCOT Region at this time will be subjected to treatment unlike that imposed on

previous industrial facilities. As a result, the costs and burdens imposed on new industrial facilities

will be greater than the costs and burdens imposed on earlier industrial facilities, the result of

which is to disadvantage new facilities and discourage siting in Texas. These changes create a

competitive moat that protects incumbent industries and introduces unknown costs on new sources

of jobs and economic growth. When it enacted SB 6, the Texas Legislature required the

Commission to “establish standards for interconnecting large load customers in the ERCOT power

region in a manner designed to support business development in this state while minimizing the

potential for stranded infrastructure costs and maintaining system reliability.” 13 Subjecting new

large industrial facilities that have a peak demand that exceeds 75 MW to higher costs than have

been imposed on earlier industrial large facilities that have a peak demand that exceeds 75 MW is

antithetical to the Commission’s policy guidance in PURA § 37.0561(b). As a result, and given

the data recently shown by ERCOT that non-LCL load requests are approximately one percent

(1%) of ERCOT’s current large load interconnection process backlog, Eolian respectfully submits

that a large industrial facility that is not a large data center or “large computational load” as

discussed in Question No. 4, should not be subject to these new proposed cost structures, but

instead, should be subject to the same transmission cost allocation as applied to all other large

industrial facilities in the ERCOT Region.

                                          CONCLUSION

        Eolian appreciates the opportunity to comment on the proposed rules and respectfully

requests that the Commission adopt rules consistent with these comments. The Commission’s final



13
     PURA § 37.0561(b).


                                                                           Eolian Comments – Page 11
 rule as adopted will directly affect the development of a domestic industrial metal production

facility that is needed to address critical U. S. security issues, including whether this facility will

be able to locate in the ERCOT region under the Commission’s modified cost allocation policy

framework.

                                               Respectfully submitted,

                                               /s/ Aaron Zubaty
                                               _________________________________________
                                               Aaron Zubaty
                                               Chief Executive Officer
                                               Eolian, L.P.
                                               aaron@eolianenergy.com
                                               (650) 744-2100

                                                                           Eolian Comments – Page 12
                                        PROJECT NO. 58000

 RULEMAKING TO UPDATE                              §       PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION
 WHOLESALE AND IOU RETAIL                          §                OF TEXAS
 TRANSMISSION COST RECOVERY                        §
 IN THE ERCOT REGION

                                 COMMENTS OF EOLIAN, L.P
                                   EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

        The proposed amendments will directly and disproportionately impact existing and future
“large load customers” and “critical load industrial customers” that are not data centers. It is critical
that any changes in policy designed to limit data center cost impacts avoid having the inadvertent
impact of stifling the investment underway in building out the tangible economy. It is imperative
that the Commission adopt policies that differentiate all data center and data center-adjacent “large
load customers” – i.e., those loads that have created a cost-allocation problem to be solved through
this rulemaking – from the rest of the large load customers that are seeking to develop in Texas.
Commission policy amendments must recognize that some industries that are willing to pay
extraordinarily high all-in prices for electricity must not inhibit growth across the remainder of the
Texas economy.

Response to Question 1
   • The implementation of minimum charges based solely on peak demand or even on
      exposure to NCP demand creates a disincentive to adjust load exposure during the most
      critical hours on the grid. Further, if the minimum billing demand cost is a very large
      proportion of the overall annual transmission charges, this question is far more relevant
      than if the fixed costs are 10% or less of annual transmission charges. It is also critical that
      all incumbent large loads are treated the same as new entrants for any large load minimum
      billing; otherwise this rule change results in instantly better economics for incumbents than
      for new entrants.

Response to Question 2

    •   Eolian prefers option b, which would reduce the charge in phases over a 20-year
        period. Eolian respectfully submits that a new large industrial facility that is not a data
        center should not be subject to a different transmission cost allocation than is applied to all
        other large industrial facilities in the ERCOT Region. If all large industrial facilities will
        be subject to these new cost allocation requirements, then the minimum large load demand
        charge should be set as a temporary recovery mechanism for incremental, front-loaded,
        customer-caused costs and risks that objectively diminish over time.




                                                                            Eolian Comments – Page 13
 Response to Question 4

   •   Eolian’s facility is not a large data center but has been directly impacted by the focus on
       those projects. The processes that the Commission and ERCOT have been adopting to large
       data centers are not appropriate for the development of large industrial facilities. The costs
       and burdens imposed on new industrial facilities are greater than the costs and burdens
       imposed on earlier facilities, the result of which is to disadvantage new facilities. When it
       enacted SB 6, the Texas Legislature required the Commission to “establish standards for
       interconnecting large load customers in the ERCOT power region in a manner designed to
       support business development in this state while minimizing the potential for stranded
       infrastructure costs and maintaining system reliability.” Subjecting new large industrial
       facilities that have a peak demand that exceeds 75 MW to higher costs than have been
       imposed on earlier large facilities that have a peak demand that exceeds 75 MW is
       antithetical to the Commission’s policy guidance in PURA § 37.0561(b). As a result,
       Eolian respectfully submits that a large industrial facility that is not a large data center or
       “large computational load” as discussed in Question No. 4, should not be subject to these
       new proposed cost structures but instead should be subject to the same transmission cost
       allocation as applied to all other large industrial facilities in the ERCOT Region.

1.     Should the values associated with the large load minimum billing demand provisions
       be different for large load customers with different contracted peak demands or
       different non-coincident (NCP) demands?

       Yes, ifthe Commission retains a large load minimum billing demand, the applicable values

should be calibrated to the cost and stranded-infrastructure risk presented by the customer rather

than imposed as a uniform 100% floor based solely on contracted peak demand or NCP demand.

Different load sizes and operating profiles can create materially different risks, but load size alone

is not a sufficient proxy for cost causation. The Commission should use objective criteria that

account for the customer's reserved capacity, expected ramp, directly assigned interconnection

costs, financial security, and demonstrated operating characteristics.

       The implementation of minimum charges based solely on peak demand or exposure to NCP

demand would create a disincentive to adjust load exposure during the most critical hours of the

day. For example, if a large baseload industrial facility can adjust its load during a critical morning

during a winter storm but is charged a flat annual minimum billing demand amount based on peak

annual demand, the facility will have less incentive to adjust its processes for those critical peak

hours even though their demand reduction actions would provide a disproportionate value to grid

reliability and would help keep energy costs lower during the whether event.

       The proposed formula in § 25.193(d)(2) would set the minimum billing demand at the

greatest of contracted peak demand, the highest NCP demand in the preceding year, or 12CP

demand. For a new proj ect, contracted peak demand may therefore become the effective floor

before the proj ect has established any operating history. Combined with proposed §§ 25.193(d)(3)

and 25.252(e), which commence billing when capacity is available rather than when the customer

has energized or reached its expected load, the proposal could require a new industrial customer

        A contracted demand floor can also weaken efficient demand response incentives. If an

industrial facility can reduce grid imports during critical periods but remains billed at its contracted

peak demand, the customer receives little or no transmission cost benefit from reducing demand

when the system is stressed. The same concern applies to investments in onsite generation, storage,

load controls, or other measures that lower the customer's net transmission usage. Eolian's

comments in Project No. 58484 emphasized that transmission rate design should preserve

incentives for efficient system use and should recognize mitigation measures that reduce system

impacts.4 The Commission should preserve those incentives here rather than convert the minimum

billing demand into an unavoidable charge unrelated to actual or mitigated system use.

        The Commission should also avoid an ongoing rate distinction based solely on whether an

industrial customer happens to be a new entrant. Direct interconnection costs for a new large load

may appropriately be assigned to that customer under PURA § 35.004(c-1) and the Commission's

interconnection rules. 5 But once similarly situated customers are taking network service, newness

alone is not a cost-causation principle for permanently allocating network transmission costs.

competitive disadvantage unrelated to differences in ongoing use of the transmission system.
